name: Body dysmorphic disorder (BDD)

lead: BDD is a clinical disorder in which a person is consumed by a perceived appearance flaw that others barely notice or cannot see.
It affects roughly 2 percent of people by community estimates and is more common in cosmetic and dermatology settings.

paras: Researchers describe a biopsychosocial origin, with checking and avoidance rituals that maintain the preoccupation.
Reviews report high rates of suicidal ideation, and cosmetic procedures rarely relieve the distress. CBT and SSRIs are the recommended treatments.

lead: Body dysmorphic disorder (BDD) is a mental disorder defined by an overwhelming preoccupation with a perceived flaw in physical appearance that is minor or not observable to others, causing distress and impairment.[1] It was moved to the obsessive-compulsive spectrum in the DSM-5 in 2013, and it includes a muscle dysmorphia subtype.[1]

Commonly reported behaviours include repeated mirror checking, comparing, reassurance seeking, camouflaging and excessive grooming.[1][2] Reviews report that cognitive behavioural therapy and SSRI medication are the recommended treatments, and that cosmetic procedures rarely resolve the distress.[1][3]
Online appearance communities use language of "flaws" and "ascension", and clinicians note overlap between appearance fixation and BDD; this entry documents the clinical picture only.
infobox: DSM-5 obsessive-compulsive and related disorders; ICD-11 6B21[1]

paras: The preoccupation can last hours daily and often focuses on skin, face, hair or body shape.[1] Many people engage in checking, camouflaging and avoidance, and comorbid depression and social anxiety are common.[1] Insight may be poor, and about one-third of cases are described as delusional.[1]

Community estimates of around 2 percent are commonly cited, with a 2025 meta-analysis estimating about 17 percent, and higher rates reported in cosmetic surgery, psychiatric and dermatology settings.[1] A US telephone survey of 2,513 adults is among the population studies.[2]

Causes are considered biopsychosocial, with a twin-based heritability estimate of 43 percent and risk factors including teasing, bullying and childhood maltreatment.[1] A cognitive-behavioural model of the disorder has been proposed.[3]
CBT and SSRIs are described as effective, and modular CBT programmes have been published.[1] A severity scale based on the Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale was developed in 1997 to rate BDD.[4]

Wikipedia reports that cosmetic surgery typically does not resolve BDD distress and recommends screening of surgical patients.[1] Suicidal ideation is reported at high rates, with studies cited up to 69 percent for ideation.[1]
Enrico Morselli described "dysmorphophobia" in 1886, BDD entered the DSM in 1987 and was moved to the obsessive-compulsive spectrum in 2013.[1]
Clinical research includes a 1997 scale validation study in 125 people with BDD,[4] population prevalence surveys,[2][5] and trials of CBT and SSRIs summarised in reviews.[1]

timeline.event: DSM-5 reclassifies BDD within obsessive-compulsive and related disorders.[1]
